newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angolan government, UNITA sign diamond deal.
newsitem.headline: Angolan government, UNITA sign diamond deal.

text.p: The Angolan government and the former rebel movement UNITA have signed a deal granting the latter two diamond concessions in the country's central and southern provinces, a government mining official said on Wednesday.
He said the deal was approved at the end of May by the Council of Ministers, headed by Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos.
"UNITA's SGM company was granted concessions in the Mussende area in Bie (central province) and in Calai in Cuando Cubango (southern province)," the official told Reuters.

The government and UNITA this week convened a national unity parliament first elected in 1992, but stalled repeatedly by hitches in the fragile peace process which ended 20 years of civil war between them. Distrust still runs deep.
The Bie concession, rich in alluvial diamonds, lies between Cangandala and Nhareia towns and includes UNITA's stronghold of Andulo, home to its leader Jonas Savimbi.
In the south, the concession runs between Mupupa and Calai on the border with Namibia.
There has been no exploration yet in these two areas, and UNITA is seeking to hold on to its alluvial-rich areas in the Cuango River valley in Lunda Norte.
Despite Angola's political settlement, UNITA continues to hold most of the countryside including a significant share of the country's rich diamond resources.

However, UNITA has lost a key ally in former Zairean president Mobutu Sese Seko, who was toppled from power last month. His regime provided logistics and bases for the movement for years on Zairean territory and also helped UNITA market its diamonds.
Seizing its opportunity, the dos Santos government began military strikes on UNITA-occupied areas in Lunda Norte province several weeks ago, threatening the goal of national reconciliation.

U.N. military sources said the government's military build-ups at Cafunfo, Dundo, Saurimo and Malange were aimed at putting "psychological" pressure on UNITA to give up control of the diamond wealth and allow extension of state rule to the entire country.
They said however, the government has suffered heavy losses in battles south of the mining town of Nzage.

Mining sources meantime told Reuters that UNITA's representatives in a joint peace commission had last November signed an agreement to negotiate for a stake in concessions held by the International Defence and Security (IDAS) company, and a consortium including Brazil's Odebrecht.
